road.driveNote: There is no drivable public road to the Copper Creek trailhead. Most parties drive to Chelan and take the Lake Chelan Boat Company ferry (~4 hr) to Lucerne, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up Railroad Creek Road (closed to public vehicles) to Holden Village (3,200 ft). The alternative is driving to the Phelps Creek/Trinity trailhead and hiking ~11 miles over Spider Gap and down Railroad Creek to Holden.
road.seasonalGate: As of a December 2025 storm that caused catastrophic landslide damage to Forest Service Road 8301 between the Lucerne dock and Holden Village, the USFS has closed FSR 8301 and Holden Village to all guests under an emergency closure order (effective through at least Dec 31, 2027, per the Chelan/Entiat Ranger District alert); Holden Village's own site confirms no 2026 guest season and an uncertain reopening timeline. The boat-and-shuttle approach described here is NOT currently available - the Spider Gap cross-country route from the Phelps Creek/Trinity trailhead is the only remaining line, and it is snow-covered and avalanche-prone outside summer and fall. That is not a drive-to alternative either: FR 6200 is gated at milepost 18.2 past Atkinson Flat under USFS order #06-17-07-2026-11, cutting off both the Phelps Creek and Trinity trailheads, so the Spider Gap approach itself now begins with several miles of closed road. Confirm current status with the Chelan Ranger District before planning this trip.

approach: Traditionally approached via the Carbon River Road to Ipsut Creek and the Carbon Glacier — but SR-165's Fairfax Bridge (the only public access to Carbon River) was permanently closed by WSDOT in April 2025 with no detour, making this a ~19-mile one-way wilderness approach via the Wonderland Trail. Many recent parties instead approach via White River/Glacier Basin, crossing the Winthrop Glacier over Curtis Ridge to reach the base of the wall.

approach: With the historic Staircase (North Fork Skokomish) approach closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, the practical way in is now from the Duckabush Trailhead via Duckabush Trail #803. The tread starts easy for about 2.4 miles to Little Hump, then climbs the steep, loose-rock switchbacks of Big Hump before mellowing again to the Olympic National Park boundary around mile 6.2-6.7. Continue up the valley past 5 Mile Camp (a popular fishing/camping flat by the river) and 10 Mile Camp (~mile 12), where the trail's grade eases through old-growth forest along the Duckabush River — reliable water the whole way, though treat it. Beyond 10 Mile Camp the trail steepens again through the rougher upper-valley tread toward the Duckabush Camp junction with the O'Neil Pass/North Fork Skokomish Trail; from there it's a tough, sustained climb — the last mile notably steep — up to Marmot Lake (roughly 20-21 miles from the trailhead), a good base camp near Hart Lake (0.9 mi), Lake LaCrosse (1.4 mi), and O'Neil Pass (1.2 mi). From Marmot Lake, drop back to the Home Sweet Home junction and climb the connector trail over First Divide (4,688 ft) — the old link to the closed Staircase side — then leave maintained trail to angle cross-country/climber's-path up open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Given the mileage (~29 miles one-way), most parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a camp at Marmot Lake or Home Sweet Home rather than a car-to-car push.

approach_variants.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
approach_variants.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, so the practical way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer
Rockfall in the gully system onto anyone below
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed Skokomish corridor
A very long, remote walk-out from anywhere on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

approach: Start at the Duckabush Trailhead (FR 2510-060) off US 101 and follow the Duckabush River Trail #803. The first real test is Big Hump at mile 3.9: a steep, loose-rock push of about 1,000 ft in roughly 30 switchbacks, then a 800 ft drop back down to river level on the far side — this is the trail's technical crux underfoot, not the summit. Continue upriver through old growth and a burned section (standing dead snags — use caution in wind) to Five Mile Camp (5.3 mi), a popular water stop and camp at a set of rapids. Between the Olympic National Park boundary (~6.2 mi from the trailhead) and Ten Mile Camp expect scattered blowdown and a documented trail washout that must be scrambled around rather than crossed directly. Around mile 17, just before Duckabush Camp, the trail fords the Duckabush River itself — a wide crossing that can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain; scout upstream/downstream for the best braid and use a pole. From Duckabush Camp, continue upvalley roughly 3 more miles on the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass trail; the unmarked Marmot Lake climbers' route then leaves the maintained trail (no sign, occasional cairns at best) and follows a small feeder creek up climber's-left into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of Mount Steel's summit. This final stretch is cross-country travel over heather benches and talus, finishing on easy Class 2 slopes to the summit ridge and the 6,225-ft high point. Snow lingers in the amphitheater and on the upper slopes into summer, with nasty cornices reported on the summit ridge until late June, so carry an ice axe and expect firm early-morning snow before roughly early July. Water is reliable along the Duckabush and at Marmot Lake but scarce once you leave the creek for the amphitheater, so top off there. With Marmot Lake itself over 21 miles from the trailhead, this route is done as a multi-day backpack with a high camp at Marmot Lake or the amphitheater, not a car-to-car day climb. A second, reportedly easier approach starts from First Divide (13-14 miles from the Staircase trailhead via the North Fork Skokomish Trail): follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake, drop southwest to the saddle between Mount Steel's two summit humps, then finish north along the summit ridge; this line shares the same early-summer cornice/avalanche caution near the ridge crest.
